spatialCoverage.description: The dataset covers rivers ranging in latitude from New Zealand (46 degree S) to the high Arctic (70.5) (see GlobalErosionLocations.png). The majority of studies were conducted in the mid-latitudes with a large fraction being conducted in the United States, Cananda, and the United Kingdom. There are few studies in Africa or the Asian Arctic.

measurementTechnique:
This dataset is a compilation of 993 measurements of riverbank erosion or migration rates from 336 rivers and streams compiled from 169 published English language studies. The dataset spans rivers across latitudes ranging from 46 deg south to 71 deg north. The rivers range in drainage area from 0.6 to 3 million square kilometers. If provided in a published study, recorded channel width, river drainage area, and sediment load and/or yield were summarized. In the absence of these ancillary data from the original source, this data was compiled from other published studies, global and regional datasets, or measured from Google Earth images. The dataset also provides information on whether the rates were measured at an individual river bend or represent reach-based averages, as well as, whether the river is single or multi-threaded.
The contributing drainage area above each segment was determined using a combination of the HydroBasins level-12 watershed polygons (Lehner & Grill, 2013) and MERIT-Hydro upstream drainage area grid (Yamazaki et al., 2019). There values are reported in the DrainageArea(km^2)_rabpro field.
In addition to values reported in the source publications for erosion rates, mean annual water discharge and sediment yields were computed from the global, annual WBMsed estimates of long-term sediment flux (Cohen et al., 2013). Because WBMsed accumulates sediment estimates downstream, the maximum sediment flux pixel, i.e. the most-downstream pixel, was selected within each segment’s drainage basin. The time series of annual water discharge and sediment fluxes at each of these pixels were averaged over the timespan of measured erosion or migration, or between 1980-2010 if the erosion or measured migration occurred outside the 30-year window of WBMsed simulations. Monthly maximum flow values were obtained from the FLO1K dataset (Barbaross et al., 2018). These values were extracted using rabpro (Schwenk et al., 2022) and averaged for both the entire length of the FLO1K dataset (1960-2015) and for the time interval associated with the individual erosion rate measurements.
RiverSlope_rabpro– We used rabpro (Schwenk et al., 2022) to map each bank erosion observation to its corresponding flowline in MERIT-Hydro. Slopes were computed as E_u - E_d / (s_d - s_u) for E=elevation, u = upstream, d = downstream, and s = along-channel distance. E_u and E_d are chosen to be the minimum of 10 channel widths upstream and downstream or 10 km (upstream and downstream) of the measurement location. Exceptions were made in cases of slope breaks (e.g. at confluences). This reach-averaged slope accounts for variability and noise in the MERIT-Hydro flowline elevation profile. River slopes were also extracted from the Lin et al. 2020 global data product.
Barbarossa, V., Huijbregts, M. A. J., Beusen, A. H. W., Beck, H. E., King, H., & Schipper, A. M. (2018). Lehner, B., and Grill, G., 2013, Global river hydrography and network routing: baseline data and new approaches to study the world’s large river systems: Hydrological Processes, v. 27, p. 2171–2186, doi:DOI: 10.1002/hyp.9740 Global.

List of Fields in data set:
River Name of River
River_ID Name of unique data record, for some rivers multiple erosion rates are reported for which unique locations and ancillary data, such as drainage area, width, or discharge may be available
Location State or country of the study site
Latitude Latitude reported by study or best estimated location based on information supplied in publication
Longitude Longitude reported by study or best estimated location based on information supplied in publication
Erosion Reference Citation for the published erosion rates
Erosion Rate (m/yr) Linear erosion or migration rate reported in published study
Total Erosion Time(yr) Time period over which the erosion rate was measured
StartYear Beginning year for the eroison rate measurement
EndYear End year for the eroison rate measurement
LocalvReach L indiciates that the published erosion rate is based on a study of a small portion of the river, typically an indiidual bank or bend. R indicates the reported rate is the erosion or migration averaged along a reach of river typically including multiple bends or more
Channel Width (m) Reported or best available estimate for the repersentative channel width in for the location of erosion measurement
Width Reference Unless otherwise noted the source of the width is from the primary source listed under “Erosion Reference”, Google Earth indicates a representative width was deteremined using the measure tool in Google Earth based on available imagery of the study site
DrainageArea(km^2)_rabpro Area of the drainage basin upstream of the location of the erosion measurement obtained using rabpro (Schwenk et al. 2022)
DrainageArea(km^2) Drainage areas reported in the original erosion study or derived from other data sources listed in the Drainage Area Reference column
Drainage Area Reference Source of the reported drainage area, if not listed, the drainage area was obtained from the study listed for the Erosion Rate - USGS StreamStats plaftorm (https://streamstats.usgs.gov/ss/ ), GRDC values obtained from the closest GRDC gage location (https://www.bafg.de/GRDC/EN/Home/homepage_node.html)
Planform(MvsS) “M” = multi-threaded, “S” = single-threaded
Sinuosity Length of the river channel divided by the valley length in the segment of river of the erosion measurements
River_slope_pub River slople reported in the original erosion study or derived from other data sources listed in the Slope Reference column
Slope Reference Source of the reported river slope, if not listed, the river slope was obtained from the study listed for the Erosion Rate - USGS StreamStats plaftorm (https://streamstats.usgs.gov/ss/ )
RiverSlope_rabpro River slope of the location of the erosion measurement obtained using rabpro (Schwenk et al. 2022)
RiverSlope_Lin River slope obtained from the Lin et al (2020) global data product
Pub Mean Annual Q (m3_s) Published values of river discharge from either the source reference for the eroison rate or from another source if listed
PubQ Reference Unless otherwise noted the source of the width is from the primary source listed under “Erosion Reference”
FLO1K_MonthlyMax_LT FLO1K (Barbarossa et al., 2018) maximum monthly flow for each year averaged for entire time series (1960-2015), values extracted and averaged using rabpro (Schwenk et al., 2022)
FLO!K_MontlyMax_PoR FLO1K (Barbarossa et al., 2018) maximum monthly flow for each year averaged for the period of record (PoR) for the erosion measurements, values extracted and averaged using rabpro (Schwenk et al., 2022)
WBMsedMeanAnnualQ_m3_s Mean annual river discharge at the location of the erosion measurement based on the WBMSed model (Cohen et al, 2013) for the time period of the erosion measurement
SedLoad_T_yr Published values of sediment load from either the source reference for the eroison rate or from another source if listed
Published Sed Ref Unless otherwise noted the source of the width is from the primary source listed under “Erosion Reference”
PubSedimentYield T km^-2 Yr-1 Either a publlshed value of sediment or the calculated sediment yield based on published sediment load and drainage area
SedimentFlux_kg_s The maximum sediment flux pixel, i.e. the most-downstream pixel, each segment’s drainage basin based modeled WBMsed values (Cohen et al., 2013)
WBMsedSedYield T km^-2 Yr-1 The WBMsed sediment flux, on an annual basis, divided by the contributing drainage area.
KG_Zone Köppen-geiger climate classification based on Beck et al. 2018

Additional Notes:
Background image for figure showing measurement locations from Beck et al. 2018
In Donovan et al. 2015, locations of erosion measurements were best estimates based on name and figures in the paper to approximately locate.
In Langovic 2020, averaged meander rates for each section to get a reach averaged erosion rate.
For Bertalan et al. 2021, used only natural or minimally impacted reaches. Erosion rates for individual time periods averaged with time (duration) weighting to get a single erosion rate for the entire period of record. Sediment loads were linearly interpolated from upstream to downstream and converted the volumetric fluxes (m3/yr) to tonnes using a density of 2.2 gm/cm3 for suspended load.
Rates from Langat et al. 2020, were only migration rates from 1975-1986. Dams were constructed in early 1980s and caused a reduction in migration rates.
